newsitem.title: USA: Clinton said open to review of benefits pay scale.
newsitem.headline: Clinton said open to review of benefits pay scale.

text.p: The Clinton administration is willing to consider ways to scale back the annual cost-of-living adjustment used to set payments for federal benefit programmes, the Washington Post reported on Wednesday.

The newspaper quoted Laura Tyson, head of Clinton's National Economic Council, as saying: "Are we open to reviewing the issue? Yes. I think that the administration will take a serious look at this and we think the Congress should as well."

Another senior Clinton administration official told the paper there had been a subtle but significant shift in the administration's openness to modifying the consumer price index (CPI) since February.

"We are trying to signal that we are open. We aren't going to lead the train... but we're not going to be out there attacking somebody simply for raising the issue," the official was quoted as saying.
A congressionally appointed panel is scheduled to release a report on Wednesday stating that the consumer price index (CPI) overstates inflation by a percentage point or more.

Some Republican and Democratic legislators have argued that cost-of-living increases for Social Security pensioners and other government beneficiaries -- which are tied to the CPI -- should be reduced accordingly. That would save the government billions of dollars and help balance the budget.
But the Clinton administration has resisted that, saying that any changes in the consumer price index should be made by government statisticians, not by politicians.

On Tuesday, Labour Secretary Robert Reich told CNN television the government must be careful about altering the CPI to save money on cost-of-living increases for pensioners, veterans and other beneficiaries.
The Post also quoted Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin as saying the administration's position had not changed.
"Our position is the same as it has been for the whole time this issue has been debated," Rubin was quoted as saying.

He stressed that he had not seen the report to be released on Wednesday and that administration officials would have to study it carefully and "see how people react" before coming to any conclusions about its recommendations.
